## **Netio Python Library (PyPI)**

There is a Python 3 library called "Netio" available on PyPI that provides bindings and CLI for communication with NETIO Products devices.

### Installation
You can install it using: `pip install Netio --upgrade`

### Basic Usage
To use the library, you import Netio and create a new instance with an endpoint like: `from Netio import Netio n = Netio('http://netio-4ll.local:8080/netio.json', auth_rw=('admin', 'password'))`

### Features
- The library requires you to enable JSON API on your NETIO device
- It provides an interface to control NETIO Products devices
- Includes both a Python library and command-line interface
- Supports HTTPS with certificate verification options

The library works with NETIO's JSON HTTP API protocol, which allows you to access measurements and control electrical sockets on NETIO 4x devices from third-party applications.

You can find the package at: https://pypi.org/project/Netio/

I found information about **pypjlink**, a Python library for controlling projectors using the PJLink protocol. Here are the key findings:

## Overview
pypjlink is a python library and command line utility to interoperate with projectors through pjlink protocol. PJLink is a standard for controlling data projectors.

## Installation
Latest release can be found on pypi and installed with: $ pip install (the package name is `pypjlink`).

## Command Line Usage
The library includes a command-line interface. For example:
- $ pjlink -p 10.1.1.1 power to query projector status
- $ pjlink -p 10.1.1.1 power off to send commands

## Python API Usage
from pypjlink import Projector with Projector.from_address('projector_host') as projector: projector.authenticate() projector.set_power('on')

## Project History
It is a fork of the work of Peter Ward. There are multiple active forks on GitHub, including versions by Gaetano Guerriero, benoitlouy, and jeffh0821. There's also a newer library called **pypjlink2** that Implementation of the PJLink Class 1 protocol to control projectors.

Based on the search results, I found information about Python libraries for controlling ANEL power sockets via UDP:

## pypwrctrl - Main Python Library

The primary Python library for ANEL NET-PwrCtrl devices is **pypwrctrl**, which is a library and command line utility that offers the functionality provided by the UDP protocol.

### Key Features:
- Devices can be found by network discovery and saved into a configuration file for easy access.
- The program was written on Linux but should also run on Windows, Mac OS X, and every other operating system supported by Python 3.
- The library allows controlling the state of power outlets, with turning a power outlet on as simple as using commands that change the state of specific sockets by device address.

### Availability:
- **PyPI**: https://pypi.org/project/pypwrctrl/
- **GitHub**: https://github.com/Innovailable/pypwrctrl

### Important Security Warning:
Enabling the UDP protocol is quite insane from a security standpoint, as the user credentials are transmitted as plaintext in the commands requiring authentication.

### License:
pypwrctrl is free software that can be redistributed and/or modified under the terms of the GNU General Public License as published by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or any later version.

This library appears to be the standard Python solution for controlling ANEL NET-PwrCtrl power sockets via UDP protocol in 2026.

This library appears to be the standard Python solution for controlling ANEL NET-PwrCtrl power sockets via UDP protocol in 2026.

## Getting started

To make it easy for you to get started with GitLab, here's a list of recommended next steps.

Already a pro? Just edit this README.md and make it your own. Want to make it easy? [Use the template at the bottom](#editing-this-readme)!

## Add your files

- [ ] [Create](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/repository/web_editor.html#create-a-file) or [upload](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/repository/web_editor.html#upload-a-file) files
- [ ] [Add files using the command line](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/gitlab-basics/add-file.html#add-a-file-using-the-command-line) or push an existing Git repository with the following command:

```
cd existing_repo
git remote add origin https://git.zkm.de/MuTech/software/control-units/mutech-control/anel-runner.git
git branch -M main
git push -uf origin main
```

## Integrate with your tools

- [ ] [Set up project integrations](https://git.zkm.de/MuTech/software/control-units/mutech-control/anel-runner/-/settings/integrations)

## Collaborate with your team

- [ ] [Invite team members and collaborators](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/members/)
- [ ] [Create a new merge request](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/merge_requests/creating_merge_requests.html)

- [ ] [Set auto-merge](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/merge_requests/merge_when_pipeline_succeeds.html)

## Test and Deploy

Use the built-in continuous integration in GitLab.

- [ ] [Get started with GitLab CI/CD](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/quick_start/index.html)
- [ ] [Analyze your code for known vulnerabilities with Static Application Security Testing (SAST)](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/application_security/sast/)
- [ ] [Deploy to Kubernetes, Amazon EC2, or Amazon ECS using Auto Deploy](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/topics/autodevops/requirements.html)
- [ ] [Use pull-based deployments for improved Kubernetes management](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/clusters/agent/)
- [ ] [Set up protected environments](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/environments/protected_environments.html)

***

# Editing this README

When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is just a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.

## Suggestions for a good README

Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects. Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.

## Name
Choose a self-explaining name for your project.

## Description
Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.

## Badges
On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add some to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.

## Visuals
Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools like ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.

## Installation
Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that whoever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as quickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.

## Usage
Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while providing links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.

## Support
Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.

## Roadmap
If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.

## Contributing
State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.

For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should run or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.

You can also document commands to lint the code or run tests. These steps help to ensure high code quality and reduce the likelihood that the changes inadvertently break something. Having instructions for running tests is especially helpful if it requires external setup, such as starting a Selenium server for testing in a browser.

## Authors and acknowledgment
Show your appreciation to those who have contributed to the project.

## License
For open source projects, say how it is licensed.

## Project status
If you have run out of energy or time for your project, put a note at the top of the README saying that development has slowed down or stopped completely. Someone may choose to fork your project or volunteer to step in as a maintainer or owner, allowing your project to keep going. You can also make an explicit request for maintainers.

content.thinking:
Great! Now I have clear requirements. Let me think through the ON command staggering options carefully.

For ON commands, we need to prevent:
1. Power spikes (electrical load)
2. Network congestion (especially for PJLink)
3. Device overload

The user has:
- Multiple exhibitions
- Multiple artworks per exhibition
- Multiple devices per artwork
- Devices can be: ANEL, NETIO (3 ports per IP), PJLink projectors, Shell commands

Let me think of sane options for ON command staggering:

Option 1: Global queue (one at a time)
- Safest for power
- Slowest (100 devices = 500 seconds = 8+ minutes)
- But respects per-device cooldowns

Option 2: Per device-type queues
- NETIO queue (5s stagger)
- PJLink queue (longer stagger, like 10s)
- ANEL queue (5s stagger)
- Shell queue (instant or 1s stagger)
- Faster than global
- Still respects electrical concerns per type

Option 3: Per-IP queues
- Each unique IP gets its own queue
- NETIO with 3 ports on same IP: wait 5s between each port
- Different IPs can run in parallel
- Fast but might cause power spikes if many devices

Option 4: Artwork-level parallelization
- Within an artwork: sequential with stagger
- Different artworks: can run in parallel
- Assumption: artworks are on different circuits
- Good balance

Option 5: Smart hybrid
- Group devices by "power domain" (configured)
- Within power domain: sequential with stagger
- Different power domains: parallel
- Most flexible but needs configuration

Option 6: Simple delay pool
- Max N concurrent operations (e.g., 5)
- Each operation takes min 5s
- Simple, effective, doesn't need complex grouping


- Options 2, 4, and 6 seem most practical to present.

For the database side, they need something that scales to handle 1000 devices across hundreds of artworks and dozens of exhibitions, with enable/disable controls at every level. SQLite works well for single-server setups and can easily manage this scale with proper indexing. The schema should include exhibitions, artworks, and devices/units tables with hierarchy relationships and enabled flags throughout.

I'd also track device states separately to capture current status and last activity, plus optionally log command history for auditing purposes.

- NETIO devices: 5s stagger between each
- PJLink devices: 10s stagger (more fragile)

**Pros:** Simple, respects device characteristics
**Cons:** All NETIO devices sequential even if on different circuits
**Use case:** "Turn on Exhibition A" → all NETIO wait 5s each, all projectors wait 10s each

### Option 2: Artwork-Level Parallelization
```
- Artworks execute in parallel
- Within each artwork: devices sequential with 5s stagger
```
**Pros:** Assumes artworks are on different electrical circuits (usually true)
**Cons:** If multiple artworks share a circuit, could spike
**Use case:** Exhibition with 10 artworks → all start simultaneously, but each artwork's 5 devices go one-by-one

### Option 3: Concurrent Limit with Delay Pool
```
- Max N devices simultaneously (e.g., 5)
- Each device ON takes minimum 5s slot
- Per-device cooldowns still respected
```
**Pros:** Simple, predictable, no complex grouping
**Cons:** Might still hit same circuit multiple times
**Use case:** "Turn on all" → max 5 devices powering on at any moment, rolling window

### Option 4: Smart Hybrid (Most Flexible)
```
- Devices tagged with "power_zone" in config/DB
- Same power zone: sequential with stagger
- Different power zones: parallel
- Per-device cooldowns always respected
```
**Pros:** Most accurate, handles complex installations
**Cons:** Needs configuration, more complex
**Use case:** You configure "Gallery 1 Circuit A", "Gallery 1 Circuit B" - each circuit sequential, different circuits parallel

## My Recommendation

Start with **Option 3 (Concurrent Limit)** for simplicity:
- Set `max_concurrent_on_commands: 5` in config
- Set `on_command_stagger_delay: 5s` in config
- Later add **Option 4** if needed for complex installations

This gives you safety without needing complex power zone configuration upfront.

## Database Design

**PostgreSQL** or **SQLite**?
- SQLite: Fine for 1000 devices on single server, simpler deployment
- PostgreSQL: Better for multi-server, more robust, better tooling

I'd suggest **PostgreSQL** for production (better for 1000 devices, concurrent access, backups) but **SQLite** works too if single-server deployment.

## Key Best Practices

### Concurrency Control
Python provides a Semaphore construct to synchronize concurrent workers and manage an internal counter decremented by each acquire() call. You can tune the number of concurrent workers by changing the limit in the asyncio.Semaphore object.

### General Best Practices
Use asyncio.create_task() for background coroutines and keep references to avoid garbage collection, close sessions and resources cleanly using async with, and use timeouts and retry policies for network reliability.

### When to Use Asyncio
For I/O-bound problems, use asyncio when you can, threading or concurrent.futures when you must, as asyncio can provide the best speed-up though some libraries haven't been ported to take advantage of it. Use asyncio when your application spends significant time waiting on I/O operations and you want to run many tasks concurrently without creating extra threads or processes.

### Common Pitfalls to Avoid
Avoid blocking I/O directly inside async code; use aiofiles or run_in_executor. Creating many ClientSession objects leads to resource exhaustion - use shared sessions. Blocking CPU-bound code should not be called directly, as it would delay all concurrent asyncio Tasks and IO operations.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive comparison of FastAPI vs Flask for REST API development in Python, focusing on async performance in 2026:

## Performance Benchmarks

FastAPI significantly outperforms Flask in benchmarks, achieving 15,000–20,000 requests per second versus Flask's 2,000–3,000. A FastAPI application using async capabilities and Uvicorn can handle around 20,000+ requests per second in benchmarks, while a Flask app using Gunicorn typically handles 4,000 to 5,000 requests per second on the same hardware.

## Async Support

FastAPI's speed is largely because ASGI is the server in which it was built and it supports asynchronous code. FastAPI has the advantage of handling requests asynchronously by declaring endpoints with the async keyword before a function.

In contrast, Flask uses the WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface) protocol, which defines how Python web applications communicate with web servers, and this synchronous design means each request occupies a worker until completion. Flask can implement asynchronous request handling with newer versions and third-party tools, but it's not first-class like in FastAPI, making Flask apps slower than FastAPI when processing concurrent requests.

## Community Adoption in 2025-2026

Flask has 68,000 GitHub stars and FastAPI has 78,000, with neither path being a dead end. FastAPI's popularity skyrocketed from just 15,000 stars in 2020 to over 78,000 stars in 2025, and according to the 2025 Python Developers Survey by JetBrains, FastAPI is now competing with Django and Flask for market leadership.

## When to Choose Each Framework

**Choose FastAPI for:**
- I/O-heavy workloads like parallel API calls, WebSocket streams, or applications handling thousands of concurrent connections
- API-first machine learning services such as model-as-a-service or real-time recommendations, as it provides better support for concurrency and async I/O operations

**Choose Flask for:**
- Building a simple ML model that takes web form input and returns a prediction, or rendering dashboards along with serving your model, making it easier to build MVPs and prototypes
- Projects valuing existing muscle memory and its decade-old extension ecosystem, giving control over every import

## Key Advantages

**FastAPI advantages:**
- Automatic validation, type safety, and live API documentation out of the box
- Used by companies like Uber, Microsoft, Hugging Face, Shopify, Airbnb, and ByteDance (TikTok)

**Flask advantages:**
- 14 years of battle-tested extensions and instant Stack Overflow answers

The search results consistently show that for 2026, FastAPI is the superior choice for high-performance REST APIs requiring async capabilities, while Flask remains viable for simpler applications and teams preferring traditional synchronous patterns.

Perfect! I've completed my research. Here's what I found:

## Research Summary

### Python Libraries Available

**Device Control:**
- **ANEL:** [pypwrctrl](https://pypi.org/project/pypwrctrl/) - UDP control library for ANEL NET-PwrCtrl
- **PJLink:** [pypjlink](https://github.com/benoitlouy/pypjlink) - TCP control for projectors
- **NETIO:** [Netio](https://pypi.org/project/Netio/) - HTTP/JSON API client
- **Shell:** Built-in `subprocess` module (asyncio-compatible)

**Web Framework:**
- **FastAPI** is the clear winner for this use case:
  - 15-20k requests/sec vs Flask's 2-3k
  - Native async/await support (ASGI)
  - Automatic API docs (Swagger/OpenAPI)
  - Type validation built-in
  - Used by Uber, Microsoft, Netflix

**Async Best Practices:**
- Use `asyncio.Semaphore` for concurrent request limits
- Shared session objects (avoid creating multiple)
- Proper timeouts and retry policies
- `run_in_executor` for blocking I/O if needed

---

## Proposed Architecture Design

### Service Structure

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Main Service (Python/FastAPI)       │
│                                             │
│  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐ │
│  │  REST API   │  │   Device Managers    │ │
│  │             │  │                      │ │
│  │ /api/control│  │  - PJLink Manager   │ │
│  │ /api/fast   │  │  - NETIO Manager    │ │
│  │ /api/admin  │  │  - Shell Manager    │ │
│  │ /api/state  │  │  - ANEL Client      │ │
│  └─────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘ │
│         │                   │               │
│  ┌──────▼───────────────────▼────────────┐ │
│  │    Command Orchestrator               │ │
│  │  - ON stagger (1s delay)              │ │
│  │  - OFF broadcast + verify             │ │
│  │  - Per-device cooldowns               │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│         │                                   │
│  ┌──────▼───────────┐  ┌────────────────┐ │
│  │   PostgreSQL     │  │  Config        │ │
│  │   - Exhibitions  │  │  (YAML/TOML)   │ │
│  │   - Artworks     │  │  Hot-reloadable│ │
│  │   - Devices      │  └────────────────┘ │
│  │   - States/Logs  │                     │
│  └──────────────────┘                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    │ REST API (Key Auth)
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│     ANEL Runner (Python/FastAPI)            │
│                                             │
│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐  │
│  │  REST API    │  │  ANEL Manager      │  │
│  │              │  │  (pypwrctrl)       │  │
│  │ GET /state   │  │                    │  │
│  │ POST /on     │  │  UDP Protocol      │  │
│  │ POST /off    │  │                    │  │
│  └──────────────┘  └────────────────────┘  │
│                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Core Components

**1. Device Managers (Async)**
```python
class PJLinkManager:
    - async get_state(device) -> State
    - async set_power(device, on/off) -> Result
    - Per-device cooldown tracking
    - Connection pooling
    
class NETIOManager:
    - async get_state(device, port) -> State
    - async set_state(device, port, on/off) -> Result
    - HTTP session reuse
    
class ShellManager:
    - async execute_command(cmd) -> Result
    - Pattern matching for state detection
```

**2. Command Orchestrator**
```python
- execute_control_command(target, state, mode='web'|'fast')
  - Web mode: ON with 1s stagger, OFF with verification
  - Fast mode: Fire once, no retry
  
- verify_off_states(devices)
  - Check every 30s for 5 minutes
  - Retry if not off
  - "cooling" counts as success
  
- respect_cooldowns()
  - Per-device next_allowed_at timestamp
  - Configurable per device type
```

**3. State System**
```python
States:
- -1: error
-  0: off
-  1: on
-  2: cooling (counts as "off received")
-  3: warming
-  4: off_verifying (internal)
-  5: off_failed (after max retries)
```

**4. Configuration (YAML)**
```yaml
device_types:
  pjlink:
    cooldown_seconds: 30
    off_verify_interval: 30
    off_verify_duration: 300
    request_timeout: 10
    
  netio:
    cooldown_seconds: 5
    off_verify_interval: 30
    off_verify_duration: 180
    
  anel:
    cooldown_seconds: 5
    runner_url: "http://anel-runner:8001"
    runner_api_key: "xxx"

orchestrator:
  on_stagger_delay: 1.0  # seconds
  max_concurrent_requests: 10
  
database:
  url: "postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mutech"
```

**5. Database Schema**
```sql
exhibitions (id, name, enabled, ...)
artworks (id, exhibition_id, name, enabled, ...)
devices (id, artwork_id, name, type, host, port, enabled, automation, config_json, ...)
device_states (device_id, state, last_checked, next_check_allowed, ...)
command_log (id, device_id, command, source, result, timestamp, ...)
```

**6. API Endpoints**
```
Web UI:
POST /api/control/exhibition/{id}/on
POST /api/control/exhibition/{id}/off
POST /api/control/artwork/{id}/on
POST /api/control/device/{id}/on
GET  /api/state/exhibition/{id}
GET  /api/state/device/{id}

Fast Lane:
POST /api/fast/device/{id}/on
POST /api/fast/device/{id}/off
GET  /api/fast/device/{id}/state

Admin:
GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/admin/exhibitions
GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/admin/artworks
GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/admin/devices
POST /api/admin/config/reload
```

---

## Technology Stack

- **FastAPI** - Web framework
- **SQLAlchemy** - ORM with asyncio support
- **asyncpg** - PostgreSQL async driver
- **Poetry** - Dependency management
- **Pydantic** - Data validation
- **pypwrctrl** - ANEL control
- **pypjlink** - PJLink control
- **httpx** - Async HTTP client (for NETIO, ANEL runner)

---

## Key Design Decisions

1. **Single 1s stagger** for ON commands - simple, prevents power spikes
2. **OFF broadcast + verify** - ensures devices actually turn off
3. **Per-device cooldowns** - prevents PJLink blocking, respects device limits
4. **FastAPI async** - handles 100s of devices concurrently
5. **PostgreSQL** - robust for 1000 devices, good tooling
6. **REST for ANEL** - stateless, simple, secure with API key
7. **Hot-reload config** - change settings without restart

Perfect! I now have a comprehensive understanding of the frontend. Let me provide a detailed summary of my findings.

## Frontend Architecture Summary

I've completed a thorough exploration of the MuTech Control frontend codebase. Here's what I found:

### 1. **Framework & Technology Stack**
- **Framework**: React 18.2.0 with React DOM
- **UI Library**: React Bootstrap 2.5.0 (Bootstrap 5.2.1)
- **Icons**: React Bootstrap Icons
- **Build Tool**: Create React App (react-scripts 5.0.1)
- **Build Output**: Static React app served via Nginx in Docker
- **Real-time Communication**: Socket.IO 4.5.2 client
- **Configuration**: Runtime environment injection via `env.js` (window.__env__ pattern)

### 2. **Backend Communication**
- **Protocol**: Socket.IO (WebSocket-based, not REST API)
- **Connection URL**: Configured via `SOCKETIO_URL` environment variable (default: `http://localhost:3002`)
- **Initialization**: Socket connection established in `App.js` on mount
- **Events Used**:
  - `database` - Receives full database state (exhibits, works, units)
  - `changeState` - Send state changes (On/Off commands) with object and state value
  - `command` - Multi-purpose: add, delete, update operations
  - `testShellCommand` - Test shell commands with callback response
  - Direct event responses with callback functions for testing

### 3. **UI Components for Device Control**

The frontend has a hierarchical structure for controlling devices:

**Layout Structure:**
- Exhibits (top level) → Works (artworks) → Units (devices)

**Device Types (Units):**
1. **Projector**: Network projectors with password/port configuration
   - Components: `FormProjector.js`
   - Fields: host, port, password, name
   - Display: Shows as `Projector` icon + hostname
   
2. **NetIO**: Network power outlets
   - Components: `FormNetio.js`
   - Fields: host, port (0-2), name
   - Display: `Outlet` icon + "N-" prefix + device name
   
3. **Anel**: Another power outlet type
   - Components: `FormAnel.js`
   - Fields: host, port (0-2), name
   - Display: `Plug` icon + "A-" prefix + device name
   
4. **Shell**: Custom shell command execution
   - Components: `FormShell.js`
   - Fields: name, commands array (Reachable, Status, On, Off)
   - Features: Test button with 5-second timeout, debug output canvas
   - Display: `Terminal` icon + name

**Control Components:**
- `ButtonsOnOff.js` - Simple On/Off button pairs (emits `changeState` with state 1 or 0)
- `ButtonsEditDelete.js` - Edit/Delete buttons for management mode
- `UnitModalButton.js` - "Add Unit" button triggering unit creation
- `UnitForm.js` - Radio selector for unit type, delegates to specific form components

### 4. **State Display & Indicators**

**State Representation:**
- State values: `-1` (danger/error), `0` (dark/off), `1` (success/on), other (warning)
- Display: Color-coded badges showing device status
- Automation flag: Indicates if device is automated (automation=true) or manual (automation=false)

**UI Display:**
- Exhibits shown in tables with striped/bordered Bootstrap styling
- Works nested under exhibits
- Units shown as:
  - Automated units: Compact badges with tooltips
  - Manual units: Cards with more information
- Tooltips show full unit JSON on hover

### 5. **Overall Architecture & Complexity**

**Component Hierarchy:**
```
App.js
├── MainNavBar (Edit mode toggle, Send Mail button)
└── ExhibitsListContainer
    └── WorksListContainer (for each exhibit)
        └── UnitContainer (for each work)
```

**Data Flow:**
- Socket receives `database` event with full state
- State stored in ExhibitsListContainer as `db` object
- Passed down as props through component tree
- User actions emit Socket.IO events back to backend
- Frontend is largely read-only display with management operations (edit/delete/add)

**Key Features:**
- Edit Mode toggle switches between view-only and management UI
- Batch operations: Can add multiple exhibits/works via comma-separated input
- Send Mail button in navbar
- Real-time database synchronization via Socket.IO
- No local state persistence (all state from backend)
- Simple inline editing for exhibit/work names

**Complexity Assessment:**
- **Low to Medium Complexity**
- Straightforward React component structure with minimal advanced patterns
- Heavy reliance on React Bootstrap for UI (not custom styled)
- No state management library (Redux, Zustand) - uses only React hooks
- No TypeScript - plain JavaScript
- No routing - single-page view of all entities
- Limited error handling/validation
- Socket.IO patterns are basic (no acknowledgments for most operations except shell commands)

### 6. **Code Quality Notes**
- Some commented-out code and merge conflict markers in `UnitContainer.js`
- Minimal comments/documentation
- Repetitive form components (could benefit from abstraction)
- Direct DOM access in shell debug output (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`)
- Console logging left in code
- String comparison issues with React form values (noted comment about radio button handling)

### 7. **Files & Paths**

**Key Files:**
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/src/App.js` - Root component
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/src/components/ExhibitsListContainer.js` - Main data container
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/src/components/UnitContainer.js` - Device display logic
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/src/components/layout/` - UI components (buttons, modals, forms)
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/src/components/Units/` - Device-specific forms
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/Dockerfile` - Multi-stage build with Nginx
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/package.json` - Dependencies

### 8. **What Would Need Rewriting**

If you're planning a redesign:

1. **Minimal code reuse potential:**
   - All form components are device-specific and could be reused with refactoring
   - Socket.IO communication pattern is simple and transferable
   - Bootstrap UI framework could be replaced entirely

2. **Likely candidates for replacement:**
   - All form components (could use form validation library)
   - UI framework (could modernize with Next.js, Svelte, Vue, etc.)
   - Add TypeScript for better type safety
   - Implement proper state management for larger feature set
   - Add routing if app needs to grow beyond single page
   - Improve error handling and user feedback

3. **Could be preserved:**
   - Socket.IO event patterns (design is reasonable)
   - Component hierarchy (logical structure)
   - Overall data flow concept

The current frontend is a relatively simple, functional control panel that could be rebuilt in most modern frameworks without significant effort. The main asset is the understanding of how devices communicate with the backend via Socket.IO.

Excellent! Now I have a comprehensive understanding of the database schema. Let me create a detailed summary report.

## Comprehensive Database Schema and Data Model Summary

Based on my exploration of the mutech-control backend, here's a detailed analysis of the database structure:

### **1. Database Technology**

- **Type**: SQLite 3
- **Library**: `better-sqlite3` (v9.4.3)
- **Location**: `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-backend/data/mutech.db`
- **Migration**: Migrated from LowDB (JSON-based) to SQLite with migration utilities
- **Backup file exists**: `mutech copy.db`

### **2. Core Entity Structure**

The system uses a hierarchical three-level structure:

```
Exhibit (Exhibition)
  ├── Work (Artwork)
  │   ├── Unit (Device)
  │   ├── Unit
  │   └── Unit
  ├── Work
  │   └── Unit
  └── Work
```

### **3. Database Schema - Three Main Tables**

#### **EXHIBITS TABLE**
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS exhibits (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

**Fields:**
- `id`: UUID string (primary key)
- `name`: Display name of the exhibition (e.g., "LH 1/2 GamePlay", "LH 7 Panolab")
- `created_at`: Timestamp of creation

**Example Data**: 9 exhibitions in the system

---

#### **WORKS TABLE**
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS works (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_id TEXT REFERENCES exhibits(id),
  fast_trigger BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_works_parent ON works(parent_id);
```

**Fields:**
- `id`: UUID string (primary key)
- `name`: Display name of the artwork (e.g., "Bubbles", "Cicumvernting the Circle")
- `parent_id`: Foreign key reference to parent exhibit
- `fast_trigger`: Boolean flag indicating if work uses "fast path" (direct/priority control path)
- `created_at`: Timestamp of creation

**Key Feature**: `fast_trigger` flag enables fast-path processing for specific works, allowing immediate execution without queue delays (configured by `FAST_PATH_ENABLED` and `FAST_PATH_TIMEOUT`)

---

#### **UNITS TABLE**
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS units (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id TEXT REFERENCES works(id),
  host TEXT NOT NULL,
  hostname TEXT,
  ip TEXT,
  unit_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  automation BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
  active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
  args TEXT,
  state INTEGER DEFAULT -1,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_units_parent ON units(parent_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_units_active ON units(active);
CREATE INDEX idx_units_automation ON units(automation);
```

**Fields:**
- `id`: UUID string (primary key)
- `parent_id`: Foreign key reference to parent work
- `host`: IP address or hostname of the device (e.g., "192.168.232.69")
- `hostname`: DNS hostname (e.g., "panasonic-pt-d4000e-100016026.zkm.de")
- `ip`: IP address
- `unit_type`: Device type (supported types below)
- `automation`: Boolean - controls if device participates in automatic state monitoring
- `active`: Boolean - **ENABLED/DISABLED FLAG** - when false, device is disabled
- `args`: JSON string containing device-specific configuration/credentials
- `state`: Integer device state (-1 = unknown, 0 = off, 1 = on)
- `created_at`: Timestamp of creation

---

### **4. Unit Types and Device Configuration**

The system supports multiple device types:

| Unit Type | Description | Connector | Default Rate Limit | Config Args |
|-----------|-------------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
| `projector` | PJLink projectors (Panasonic, NEC) | ProjectorConnector | 1 op/sec | password, port |
| `netio` | Netio power management devices | NetioConnector | 10 op/sec | port, credentials |
| `anel` | ANEL power distribution units | AnelConnector | 2 op/sec | port, password |
| `shell` | SSH shell commands | ShellConnector | 10 op/sec | user, port, password |

**Device Configuration in `args` Field (JSON):**
```json
{
  "password": "device_password",
  "port": "specific_port_or_empty",
  "username": "optional_username",
  "timeout": "optional_timeout_ms"
}
```

Example from db.json:
```json
{
  "parentId": "8e8b7a6f-07c2-4778-962a-392b3ba69c71",
  "host": "192.168.232.69",
  "hostname": ["panasonic-pt-d4000e-100016026.zkm.de"],
  "ip": "192.168.232.69",
  "unitType": "projector",
  "automation": true,
  "active": true,
  "state": 0,
  "args": {
    "password": "panasonic",
    "port": ""
  }
}
```

---

### **5. Device State Management**

**State Values:**
- `-1`: Unknown/uninitialized state
- `0`: OFF
- `1`: ON

**State Storage:**
- Stored in `units.state` column as INTEGER
- Updated by `updateUnitState()` method
- State changes can trigger cooldown mechanisms to prevent excessive polling

**State Persistence:**
- Automatically persists to SQLite database
- Synced periodically to frontend via Socket.IO (`DB_SYNC_INTERVAL`: 30 seconds default)

---

### **6. Enabled/Disabled Control Flags**

The system provides **two flags** for controlling device operation:

| Flag | Field | Default | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|---------|
| **active** | `units.active` | TRUE | Master on/off flag; when FALSE, device is completely disabled |
| **automation** | `units.automation` | TRUE | Controls if device participates in automatic state monitoring timers |

**Behavior:**
- `active = FALSE`: Device is disabled and ignored by all systems
- `automation = FALSE`: Device is enabled but not included in automatic state polling timers
- Both must be TRUE for full participation in the control system

---

### **7. Database Indexing**

Optimized for common queries:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_works_parent ON works(parent_id);        -- Find works by exhibit
CREATE INDEX idx_units_parent ON units(parent_id);        -- Find units by work
CREATE INDEX idx_units_active ON units(active);           -- Filter active devices
CREATE INDEX idx_units_automation ON units(automation);   -- Filter auto-managed devices
```

---

### **8. Related Configuration (from .env)**

The database behavior is controlled by environment variables:

```
# State Monitoring
UNCHANGED_STATE_MULTIPLIER=1.5          # Cooldown when state unchanged
MAX_UNCHANGED_CHECKS=5                  # Max unchanged checks before capping
FAILURE_COOLDOWN_MULTIPLIER=2.0         # Cooldown multiplier on failure

# Device-Specific Intervals (milliseconds)
PROJECTOR_BASE_INTERVAL=60000           # 60 seconds
NETIO_BASE_INTERVAL=30000               # 30 seconds
ANEL_BASE_INTERVAL=40000                # 40 seconds
SHELL_BASE_INTERVAL=5000                # 5 seconds

# Queue System (Rate Limiting)
QUEUE_MAX_OPERATIONS_PER_SECOND=20      # Global limit
PROJECTOR_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10         # Per device type
NETIO_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10
MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_DEVICE=1             # One operation per device at a time

# Fast Path
FAST_PATH_ENABLED=true                  # Enable fast path control
FAST_PATH_TIMEOUT=1000                  # Max time for fast path (1 second)
```

---

### **9. Data Model Relationships**

```
Exhibit (1) ──── (Many) Work
  ↓
  One exhibit can have multiple works
  
Work (1) ──── (Many) Unit
  ↓
  One work can have multiple units (devices)
  
Unit (1) ────── Device Control
  ↓
  Each unit maps to one physical device
```

**Cascade Behavior:**
- Deleting an exhibit cascades to delete all its works and units
- Deleting a work cascades to delete all its units

---

### **10. API/Socket.IO Data Flow**

**Database Access Methods:**
```javascript
// READ operations (return camelCase objects)
db.getExhibits()                    // All exhibits
db.getWorks()                       // All works
db.getUnits()                       // All units
db.getWorksByExhibit(exhibitId)    // Works in an exhibit
db.getUnitsByWork(workId)          // Units in a work
db.getAutomationUnits()            // Only automation=TRUE and active=TRUE units

// WRITE operations
db.addExhibit(exhibit)
db.addWork(work)
db.addUnit(unit)
db.updateUnit(id, unit)
db.updateUnitState(id, state)      // Fast state update
db.deleteExhibit(id)               // Cascading delete
```

**Field Naming Convention:**
- Database: snake_case (`parent_id`, `unit_type`, `fast_trigger`)
- API/JavaScript: camelCase (`parentId`, `unitType`, `fastTrigger`)
- Conversion happens in `parseExhibit()`, `parseWork()`, `parseUnit()` methods

---

### **11. Sample Real Data**

From the actual database:

**Exhibit:**
```json
{
  "id": "403e804e-8e04-4a3d-960f-21f95533e7b2",
  "name": "LH 1/2 GamePlay",
  "createdAt": "2025-06-09T..."
}
```

**Work:**
```json
{
  "id": "8e8b7a6f-07c2-4778-962a-392b3ba69c71",
  "name": "Bubbles",
  "parentId": "403e804e-8e04-4a3d-960f-21f95533e7b2",
  "fastTrigger": false,
  "createdAt": "2025-06-09T..."
}
```

**Unit (Device):**
```json
{

Excellent! Now I have a comprehensive understanding of the database schema. Let me create a detailed summary report.

## Comprehensive Database Schema and Data Model Summary

Based on my exploration of the mutech-control backend, here's a detailed analysis of the database structure:

### **1. Database Technology**

- **Type**: SQLite 3
- **Library**: `better-sqlite3` (v9.4.3)
- **Location**: `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-backend/data/mutech.db`
- **Migration**: Migrated from LowDB (JSON-based) to SQLite with migration utilities
- **Backup file exists**: `mutech copy.db`

### **2. Core Entity Structure**

The system uses a hierarchical three-level structure:

```
Exhibit (Exhibition)
  ├── Work (Artwork)
  │   ├── Unit (Device)
  │   ├── Unit
  │   └── Unit
  ├── Work
  │   └── Unit
  └── Work
```

### **3. Database Schema - Three Main Tables**

#### **EXHIBITS TABLE**
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS exhibits (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

**Fields:**
- `id`: UUID string (primary key)
- `name`: Display name of the exhibition (e.g., "LH 1/2 GamePlay", "LH 7 Panolab")
- `created_at`: Timestamp of creation

**Example Data**: 9 exhibitions in the system

---

#### **WORKS TABLE**
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS works (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_id TEXT REFERENCES exhibits(id),
  fast_trigger BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_works_parent ON works(parent_id);
```

**Fields:**
- `id`: UUID string (primary key)
- `name`: Display name of the artwork (e.g., "Bubbles", "Cicumvernting the Circle")
- `parent_id`: Foreign key reference to parent exhibit
- `fast_trigger`: Boolean flag indicating if work uses "fast path" (direct/priority control path)
- `created_at`: Timestamp of creation

**Key Feature**: `fast_trigger` flag enables fast-path processing for specific works, allowing immediate execution without queue delays (configured by `FAST_PATH_ENABLED` and `FAST_PATH_TIMEOUT`)

---

#### **UNITS TABLE**
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS units (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id TEXT REFERENCES works(id),
  host TEXT NOT NULL,
  hostname TEXT,
  ip TEXT,
  unit_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  automation BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
  active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
  args TEXT,
  state INTEGER DEFAULT -1,
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_units_parent ON units(parent_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_units_active ON units(active);
CREATE INDEX idx_units_automation ON units(automation);
```

**Fields:**
- `id`: UUID string (primary key)
- `parent_id`: Foreign key reference to parent work
- `host`: IP address or hostname of the device (e.g., "192.168.232.69")
- `hostname`: DNS hostname (e.g., "panasonic-pt-d4000e-100016026.zkm.de")
- `ip`: IP address
- `unit_type`: Device type (supported types below)
- `automation`: Boolean - controls if device participates in automatic state monitoring
- `active`: Boolean - **ENABLED/DISABLED FLAG** - when false, device is disabled
- `args`: JSON string containing device-specific configuration/credentials
- `state`: Integer device state (-1 = unknown, 0 = off, 1 = on)
- `created_at`: Timestamp of creation

---

### **4. Unit Types and Device Configuration**

The system supports multiple device types:

| Unit Type | Description | Connector | Default Rate Limit | Config Args |
|-----------|-------------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
| `projector` | PJLink projectors (Panasonic, NEC) | ProjectorConnector | 1 op/sec | password, port |
| `netio` | Netio power management devices | NetioConnector | 10 op/sec | port, credentials |
| `anel` | ANEL power distribution units | AnelConnector | 2 op/sec | port, password |
| `shell` | SSH shell commands | ShellConnector | 10 op/sec | user, port, password |

**Device Configuration in `args` Field (JSON):**
```json
{
  "password": "device_password",
  "port": "specific_port_or_empty",
  "username": "optional_username",
  "timeout": "optional_timeout_ms"
}
```

Example from db.json:
```json
{
  "parentId": "8e8b7a6f-07c2-4778-962a-392b3ba69c71",
  "host": "192.168.232.69",
  "hostname": ["panasonic-pt-d4000e-100016026.zkm.de"],
  "ip": "192.168.232.69",
  "unitType": "projector",
  "automation": true,
  "active": true,
  "state": 0,
  "args": {
    "password": "panasonic",
    "port": ""
  }
}
```

---

### **5. Device State Management**

**State Values:**
- `-1`: Unknown/uninitialized state
- `0`: OFF
- `1`: ON

**State Storage:**
- Stored in `units.state` column as INTEGER
- Updated by `updateUnitState()` method
- State changes can trigger cooldown mechanisms to prevent excessive polling

**State Persistence:**
- Automatically persists to SQLite database
- Synced periodically to frontend via Socket.IO (`DB_SYNC_INTERVAL`: 30 seconds default)

---

### **6. Enabled/Disabled Control Flags**

The system provides **two flags** for controlling device operation:

| Flag | Field | Default | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|---------|
| **active** | `units.active` | TRUE | Master on/off flag; when FALSE, device is completely disabled |
| **automation** | `units.automation` | TRUE | Controls if device participates in automatic state monitoring timers |

**Behavior:**
- `active = FALSE`: Device is disabled and ignored by all systems
- `automation = FALSE`: Device is enabled but not included in automatic state polling timers
- Both must be TRUE for full participation in the control system

---

### **7. Database Indexing**

Optimized for common queries:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_works_parent ON works(parent_id);        -- Find works by exhibit
CREATE INDEX idx_units_parent ON units(parent_id);        -- Find units by work
CREATE INDEX idx_units_active ON units(active);           -- Filter active devices
CREATE INDEX idx_units_automation ON units(automation);   -- Filter auto-managed devices
```

---

### **8. Related Configuration (from .env)**

The database behavior is controlled by environment variables:

```
# State Monitoring
UNCHANGED_STATE_MULTIPLIER=1.5          # Cooldown when state unchanged
MAX_UNCHANGED_CHECKS=5                  # Max unchanged checks before capping
FAILURE_COOLDOWN_MULTIPLIER=2.0         # Cooldown multiplier on failure

# Device-Specific Intervals (milliseconds)
PROJECTOR_BASE_INTERVAL=60000           # 60 seconds
NETIO_BASE_INTERVAL=30000               # 30 seconds
ANEL_BASE_INTERVAL=40000                # 40 seconds
SHELL_BASE_INTERVAL=5000                # 5 seconds

# Queue System (Rate Limiting)
QUEUE_MAX_OPERATIONS_PER_SECOND=20      # Global limit
PROJECTOR_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10         # Per device type
NETIO_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10
MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_DEVICE=1             # One operation per device at a time

# Fast Path
FAST_PATH_ENABLED=true                  # Enable fast path control
FAST_PATH_TIMEOUT=1000                  # Max time for fast path (1 second)
```

---

### **9. Data Model Relationships**

```
Exhibit (1) ──── (Many) Work
  ↓
  One exhibit can have multiple works
  
Work (1) ──── (Many) Unit
  ↓
  One work can have multiple units (devices)
  
Unit (1) ────── Device Control
  ↓
  Each unit maps to one physical device
```

**Cascade Behavior:**
- Deleting an exhibit cascades to delete all its works and units
- Deleting a work cascades to delete all its units

---

### **10. API/Socket.IO Data Flow**

**Database Access Methods:**
```javascript
// READ operations (return camelCase objects)
db.getExhibits()                    // All exhibits
db.getWorks()                       // All works
db.getUnits()                       // All units
db.getWorksByExhibit(exhibitId)    // Works in an exhibit
db.getUnitsByWork(workId)          // Units in a work
db.getAutomationUnits()            // Only automation=TRUE and active=TRUE units

// WRITE operations
db.addExhibit(exhibit)
db.addWork(work)
db.addUnit(unit)
db.updateUnit(id, unit)
db.updateUnitState(id, state)      // Fast state update
db.deleteExhibit(id)               // Cascading delete
```

**Field Naming Convention:**
- Database: snake_case (`parent_id`, `unit_type`, `fast_trigger`)
- API/JavaScript: camelCase (`parentId`, `unitType`, `fastTrigger`)
- Conversion happens in `parseExhibit()`, `parseWork()`, `parseUnit()` methods

---

### **11. Sample Real Data**

From the actual database:

**Exhibit:**
```json
{
  "id": "403e804e-8e04-4a3d-960f-21f95533e7b2",
  "name": "LH 1/2 GamePlay",
  "createdAt": "2025-06-09T..."
}
```

**Work:**
```json
{
  "id": "8e8b7a6f-07c2-4778-962a-392b3ba69c71",
  "name": "Bubbles",
  "parentId": "403e804e-8e04-4a3d-960f-21f95533e7b2",
  "fastTrigger": false,
  "createdAt": "2025-06-09T..."
}
```

**Unit (Device):**
```json
{
  "id": "a5f87d7f-9f58-400d-8d33-cbdc9089912a",
  "parentId": "8e8b7a6f-07c2-4778-962a-392b3ba69c71",
  "host": "192.168.232.69",
  "hostname": "panasonic-pt-d4000e-100016026.zkm.de",
  "ip": "192.168.232.69",
  "unitType": "projector",
  "automation": true,
  "active": true,
  "state": 0,
  "args": {
    "password": "panasonic",
    "port": ""
  },
  "createdAt": "2025-06-09T..."
}
```

---

### **12. Key Insights**

1. **Hierarchical Structure**: Clean 3-level hierarchy (Exhibit → Work → Unit) allows flexible organization of museum displays

2. **Device Configuration Security**: Credentials stored in JSON `args` field (should consider encryption for production)

3. **Flexible Control**: Two flags (`active`, `automation`) provide fine-grained control over device participation

4. **State Tracking**: Integer-based state system with -1 for unknown allows graceful handling of offline devices

5. **Performance Optimization**: Indexes on parent references and status flags enable fast filtering

6. **Migration Path**: System migrated from JSON-based LowDB to SQLite for better scalability

7. **Queue & Rate Limiting**: Device-specific rate limits prevent overwhelming slower devices like projectors

8. **Fast Path Feature**: `fastTrigger` flag enables priority control path for critical devices, bypassing normal queues

9. **Database Sync**: Frontend stays synchronized via Socket.IO with periodic full synchronization every 30 seconds

This schema provides a robust foundation for managing complex museum device control scenarios with multiple exhibits, artworks, and heterogeneous devices.

Based on my thorough exploration of the mutech-control deployment configuration, here's a comprehensive summary:

## DEPLOYMENT ARCHITECTURE & CONFIGURATION SUMMARY

### 1. CURRENT DEPLOYMENT APPROACH

**Technology Stack:**
- **Frontend:** React 18.2 with Socket.IO client, served via Nginx in Docker
- **Backend:** Express.js 4.18 with Node.js 16+
- **Database:** SQLite 3 (migration from LowDB JSON)
- **Container Orchestration:** Docker Compose (single docker-compose.yml in frontend)
- **Communication:** Socket.IO for real-time updates between frontend, backend, and runners
- **Registry:** Harbor (harbor.zkm.de/mutech)

**Key Files:**
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/docker-compose.yml` - Main deployment config
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/Dockerfile` - Multi-stage build (Node build + Nginx)
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-backend/app.js` - Backend entry point

### 2. CONTAINER ARCHITECTURE

**Planned Container Structure:**
```
mutech-main-server       (Backend API + Socket.IO coordination)
  ├─ Port: 3002 (or 8080 in production)
  ├─ Database: SQLite at ./data/mutech.db
  └─ Services: Express, Socket.IO server, Queue system, Timer system

mutech-frontend          (Nginx + React static files)
  ├─ Port: 80 (maps to 3001 locally via docker-compose)
  ├─ Base Image: nginx:alpine
  ├─ Build: Multi-stage (Node 21 build → Nginx production)
  └─ Runtime: Environment variable injection

mutech-netio-runner      (NETIO power outlet specialist)
  ├─ Type: HTTP API protocol handler
  ├─ Port: connects to main server via Socket.IO
  └─ Features: Command batching, connection pooling

mutech-pjlink-runner     (Projector control specialist)
  ├─ Type: TCP/PJLink protocol handler
  └─ Features: Connection management, state machine handling

mutech-shell-runner      (Shell command execution)
  ├─ Type: Local command execution
  └─ Features: Process isolation, timeout management

mutech-anel-runner       (ANEL UDP power strips - EXISTING)
  ├─ Type: UDP protocol handler
  ├─ Ports: 9975 (send), 9977 (receive)
  └─ Features: Status monitoring via broadcasts

mutech-debug             (Optional - monitoring & logging)
  ├─ Port: 3001 (configurable)
  └─ Purpose: Real-time system monitoring dashboard
```

### 3. ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES

**Backend Configuration (.env):**
```
# Server
HTTP_PORT=3002
HTTP_URL=http://localhost:3002
SOCKETIO=http://localhost:3002

# Database
DATABASE_PATH=./data/mutech.db
DATABASE_BACKUP_INTERVAL=3600000

# CORS
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3000,http://localhost:8080,http://localhost:3001,http://localhost:3002

# Timer Intervals (Base polling)
PROJECTOR_BASE_INTERVAL=60000         # 60 seconds
NETIO_BASE_INTERVAL=30000             # 30 seconds
ANEL_BASE_INTERVAL=40000              # 40 seconds
SHELL_BASE_INTERVAL=5000              # 5 seconds
UDP_BASE_INTERVAL=6000                # 6 seconds

# Cooldown Configuration
UNCHANGED_STATE_MULTIPLIER=1.5        # Interval multiplier when state unchanged
MAX_UNCHANGED_CHECKS=5                # Max checks before capping
MAX_COOLDOWN_INTERVAL=1800000         # 30 minutes max

# Failure Handling
FAILURE_COOLDOWN_MULTIPLIER=2.0       # Double interval per failure
MAX_FAILURE_COUNT=5                   # Stop timer after 5 failures

# Timer Behavior
TIMER_STARTUP_STAGGER=10000           # Spread startup over 10 seconds
TIMER_JITTER_PERCENT=10               # ±10% random jitter

# Queue System
QUEUE_PROCESS_INTERVAL=200            # Process queue every 200ms
QUEUE_MAX_OPERATIONS_PER_SECOND=20    # Global rate limit
QUEUE_MAX_RETRIES=3                   # Max retry attempts
QUEUE_RETRY_DELAY=30000               # 30 seconds between retries

# Per-Device Type Rate Limits
NETIO_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10
PROJECTOR_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10
ANEL_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=2
SHELL_MAX_OPS_PER_SECOND=10
MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_DEVICE=1

# Batching
NETIO_BATCH_DELAY=250                 # 250ms batching window
ENABLE_BATCHING=true

# API Performance
VISITOR_API_TIMEOUT=1000              # <1 second target for fast path
FAST_PATH_ENABLED=true

# Debug
DEBUG_ENABLED=true
DEBUG_WEB_PORT=3001
DEBUG_LOG_PERSISTENCE=false
```

**Frontend Configuration (.env):**
```
REACT_APP_SOCKETIO_URL=http://localhost:3002
REACT_APP_ENVIRONMENT=Development
REACT_APP_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:3000    # Optional
```

**NetIO Runner Configuration (.env):**
```
MAIN_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:3002         # or http://mutech-main-server:8080 in production
NETIO_DEFAULT_USER=netio
NETIO_DEFAULT_PASSWORD=netio
NETIO_REQUEST_TIMEOUT=5000
NETIO_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT=5000
NETIO_COMMAND_DELAY=300
RUNNER_RECONNECT_DELAY=5000
RUNNER_MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS=10
```

### 4. SERVICE CONFIGURATION PATTERNS

**Frontend Container:**
- Uses `docker-entrypoint.sh` for runtime environment injection
- Template-based configuration: `nginx.conf.template` and `env.js.template`
- Health check via `wget` to `/health` endpoint
- Restart policy: unless-stopped
- Volume: nginx_logs for logging

**Backend Service:**
- Initialization: `require("dotenv").config()`
- Socket.IO namespace routing:
  - `/` - Frontend real-time updates (current system)
  - `/runner-shell` - Shell command runner
  - `/runner-netio` - NETIO HTTP runner
  - `/runner-pjlink` - Projector runner
  - `/runner-anel` - ANEL UDP runner
  - `/debug` - Debug monitoring

**Runner Services:**
- All runners use Socket.IO client to connect to main server
- Configuration via environment variables
- Health check script: `healthcheck.js`
- Connection retry logic with exponential backoff
- Debug logging via `DEBUG` environment variable pattern

### 5. NETWORK SEGMENTATION FOR ANEL DEVICES

**ANEL UDP Protocol:**
- Send Port: 9975 (commands)
- Receive Port: 9977 (status broadcasts)
- Communication: UDP broadcasts for status monitoring
- Default credentials: user=`root`, password=`brotwurst`
- Features: 
  - Global command queuing to protect devices
  - Real-time status monitoring via broadcasts
  - Fast lane option for emergency commands
  - Zero external dependencies

**Device Type Isolation:**
- Each device type has dedicated runner with specialized protocol handling
- Deterministic routing by unit type (projector → PJLink runner, etc.)
- No separate database field for runner assignment
- Direct Socket.IO emission to appropriate namespace

### 6. CONFIGURATION FILE PATTERNS

**Environment Variable Pattern:**
- Centralized `.env` files per service
- `.env.example` and `.env.sample` templates for documentation
- No `.env` files in git (listed in .gitignore)
- Support for both development and production configurations

**Database Schema:**
Located in guide.md implementation docs:
```sql
exhibits (id, name, created_at)
works (id, name, parent_id, fast_trigger, created_at)
units (id, parent_id, host, unit_type, automation, active, args, state, update_interval, last_update, failure_count, last_state_change, created_at)
error_logs (id, unit_id, unit_name, artwork_name, error_type, user_message, technical_details, severity, resolved, created_at)
```

**Unique Constraints:**
- UNIQUE(host, unit_type) on units table prevents duplicate device definitions

### 7. CREDENTIALS MANAGEMENT

**Current Pattern:**
- Credentials stored in `.env` files (local development)
- Default credentials per device type:
  - NETIO: default user/password stored in runner `.env`
  - ANEL: UDP protocol doesn't use authentication
  - Shell: Local execution, no credentials needed
  - PJLink: Projector-specific authentication

**Sensitive Information:**
- `.env` files are NOT version controlled
- Database credentials: None (SQLite local file)
- API credentials: Embedded in device configurations via `args` JSON field
- No centralized secrets management system currently configured

**Security Notes:**
- No user authentication system required for current frontend
- Credentials are device-specific, passed per unit config
- HTTP protocol used locally (3002), needs HTTPS in production

### 8. KEY ARCHITECTURAL FEATURES

**Fast Path System:**
- `fast_trigger` boolean field on works table
- Bypasses normal timer queuing for visitor API
- Target: <1000ms response time
- Configuration: Direct database editing (no UI)

**Queue System:**
- Per-device-type rate limiting
- Global operation rate limiting
- Per-device concurrency control (max 1 operation at a time)
- Retry logic with exponential backoff

**Timer System:**
- Per-unit individual timers (replacing centralized polling)
- Cooldown algorithm: 50% increase after 5 min quiet, 2x after 15 min, 3x after 1 hour
- Maximum 10-minute interval cap
- Staggered startup to prevent network flooding
- Inactive units (`active = FALSE`) skip polling

**Database:**
- SQLite with better-sqlite3 for synchronous operations
- Transaction support for data consistency
- Hot-reload capability during production
- Migration strategy from LowDB JSON to SQLite

### 9. DEPLOYMENT SUMMARY

**Current State:**
- Frontend: Docker-based Nginx container with multi-stage build
- Backend: Node.js Express with SQLite database
- Runners: Separate Node.js containers per device type with Socket.IO client
- Communication: Socket.IO for all internal communication

**Production Readiness:**
- Environment variable configuration per container
- Health checks implemented
- Restart policies configured
- Logging volume mounts available
- Multi-stage Docker builds for optimized images

**File Locations:**
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-frontend/` - Frontend React + Nginx
- `/context/mutech-control/mutech-control-backend/` - Backend API server
- `/context/mutech-control/netio-runner/` - NETIO HTTP runner
- `/context/mutech-control/pjlink-runner/` - PJLink TCP runner
- `/context/mutech-control/command-runner/` - Shell command runner
- `/context/mutech-control/anel-runner/` - ANEL UDP runner (existing)
- `/context/mutech-control/guide.md` - Complete implementation guide (737 lines)

This is a microservices-based architecture designed to handle 500+ devices with specialized runners for each protocol type, featuring intelligent queuing, per-unit timers with cooldown algorithms, and fast-path support for real-time visitor interactions.

# MuTech Control System - Python Refactor Implementation Plan

## Executive Summary

Refactor the existing Node.js microservices architecture into a modern Python monolith with FastAPI, eliminating Socket.IO overhead while maintaining only the ANEL runner as a separate service due to network segmentation requirements.

**Key Changes:**
- **5 Node.js services → 2 Python services** (main + ANEL runner)
- **Socket.IO → REST API** with polling for frontend
- **React → Modern React + TypeScript** with better UI/UX
- **SQLite → PostgreSQL** for better scalability
- **Complex queue → Simple stagger + verify** pattern
- **Hot-reloadable YAML config** for operational flexibility

### 1.1 Main Service (Poetry Project)

## Phase 2: Database Design & Migration

### 2.1 PostgreSQL Schema

```sql
-- Exhibitions table
CREATE TABLE exhibitions (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Artworks table
CREATE TABLE artworks (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    exhibition_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES exhibitions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Devices table (formerly "units")
CREATE TABLE devices (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    artwork_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES artworks(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    device_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,  -- 'pjlink', 'netio', 'anel', 'shell'
    host VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    port INTEGER,

    -- Control flags
    enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,                    -- Master on/off
    automation_enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,         -- Allow in automation
    exclude_from_auto_onoff BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,   -- Exclude from "turn all on/off"

    -- Configuration (JSON)
    config JSONB DEFAULT '{}',  -- device-specific: password, timeout, commands, etc.

    -- State management
    state INTEGER DEFAULT -1,  -- -1=error, 0=off, 1=on, 2=cooling, 3=warming
    last_checked_at TIMESTAMP,
    next_check_allowed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,

    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,

    CONSTRAINT unique_device UNIQUE (host, port, device_type)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_artworks_exhibition ON artworks(exhibition_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_artwork ON devices(artwork_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_enabled ON devices(enabled);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_type ON devices(device_type);

-- Command log table
CREATE TABLE command_log (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    device_id UUID REFERENCES devices(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    command VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,  -- 'on', 'off', 'state'
    source VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,   -- 'web', 'fast', 'admin', 'verification'
    success BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    error_message TEXT,
    duration_ms INTEGER,
    timestamp TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_command_log_device ON command_log(device_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_command_log_timestamp ON command_log(timestamp);
```

**Key Design Notes:**
- `exclude_from_auto_onoff`: NEW flag for shell/reboot commands that should not participate in bulk ON/OFF
- `automation_enabled`: Determines if device is polled automatically
- `enabled`: Master switch - disabled devices are ignored completely
- `config` JSONB: Flexible storage for device-specific settings (passwords, commands, etc.)

### 3.2 Device Managers

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from typing import Literal

DeviceState = Literal[-1, 0, 1, 2, 3]  # error, off, on, cooling, warming

class DeviceManager(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    async def get_state(self, device: Device) -> tuple[bool, DeviceState, str | None]:
        """Returns (success, state, error_message)"""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    async def set_power(self, device: Device, on: bool) -> tuple[bool, DeviceState, str | None]:
        """Returns (success, new_state, error_message)"""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    async def test_connection(self, device: Device) -> tuple[bool, str | None]:
        """Returns (success, error_message)"""
        pass
```

**PJLink Manager (devices/pjlink_manager.py):**
```python
class PJLinkManager(DeviceManager):
    def __init__(self, config: dict):
        self.config = config
        self.cooldown_manager = CooldownManager()
        # Connection pool per device IP
        self._connections = {}

    async def get_state(self, device: Device) -> tuple[bool, DeviceState, str | None]:
        # Check cooldown
        if not self.cooldown_manager.is_allowed(device.id):
            next_time = self.cooldown_manager.next_allowed(device.id)
            return False, device.state, f"Cooldown active until {next_time}"

        try:
            async with timeout(self.config['request_timeout']):
                # Use pypjlink library
                projector = await self._get_projector(device)
                power_state = await projector.get_power()

                # Map PJLink states to our states
                state = self._map_pjlink_state(power_state)

                # Record successful check
                self.cooldown_manager.record_success(device.id, self.config['cooldown_seconds'])

                return True, state, None
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return False, -1, "Request timeout"
        except Exception as e:
            return False, -1, str(e)

    async def set_power(self, device: Device, on: bool) -> tuple[bool, DeviceState, str | None]:
        # Similar pattern with cooldown checking
        pass
```

class ShellManager(DeviceManager):
    async def get_state(self, device: Device) -> tuple[bool, DeviceState, str | None]:
        # Execute status command from device.config['commands']['status']
        # Parse output using onPattern/offPattern regex
        cmd = device.config['commands']['status']['cmd']
        on_pattern = device.config['commands']['status'].get('onPattern')
        off_pattern = device.config['commands']['status'].get('offPattern')

        try:
            proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_shell(
                cmd,
                stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
                stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE
            )
            stdout, stderr = await asyncio.wait_for(
                proc.communicate(),
                timeout=self.config['request_timeout']
            )

            output = stdout.decode()

            # Pattern matching
            if on_pattern and re.search(on_pattern, output):
                return True, 1, None
            elif off_pattern and re.search(off_pattern, output):
                return True, 0, None
            else:
                return True, -1, "Could not determine state from output"
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return False, -1, "Command timeout"

### 3.3 Command Orchestrator

**orchestrator/command_orchestrator.py:**
```python
class CommandOrchestrator:
    def __init__(self, db, device_managers, config):
        self.db = db
        self.device_managers = device_managers
        self.config = config
        self.state_verifier = StateVerifier(db, device_managers, config)
        self._on_semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(config['max_concurrent_on_commands'])

    async def execute_control_command(
        self,
        target_type: Literal['exhibition', 'artwork', 'device'],
        target_id: str,
        command: Literal['on', 'off'],
        source: Literal['web', 'fast']
    ) -> dict:
        """Main entry point for control commands"""

        # 1. Resolve target to list of devices
        devices = await self._resolve_target(target_type, target_id)

        # 2. Filter devices
        devices = self._filter_devices(devices, command)

        # 3. Execute command
        if source == 'web':
            if command == 'on':
                results = await self._execute_on_staggered(devices)
            else:
                results = await self._execute_off_with_verification(devices)
        else:  # fast lane
            results = await self._execute_fast(devices, command)

        return {
            "success": True,
            "devices_targeted": len(devices),
            "results": results
        }

    def _filter_devices(self, devices: list[Device], command: str) -> list[Device]:
        """Filter based on enabled flags"""
        filtered = []
        for device in devices:
            if not device.enabled:
                continue
            if device.exclude_from_auto_onoff and command in ['on', 'off']:
                continue
            filtered.append(device)
        return filtered

    async def _execute_on_staggered(self, devices: list[Device]) -> list[dict]:
        """ON commands: 1 second stagger, limited concurrency"""
        results = []

        for device in devices:
            async with self._on_semaphore:  # Limit concurrent operations
                result = await self._execute_single_device(device, 'on', 'web')
                results.append(result)

                # Stagger delay
                await asyncio.sleep(self.config['on_stagger_delay_seconds'])

        return results

    async def _execute_off_with_verification(self, devices: list[Device]) -> list[dict]:
        """OFF commands: Broadcast, then verify"""
        # 1. Send OFF to all devices in parallel
        tasks = [
            self._execute_single_device(device, 'off', 'web')
            for device in devices
        ]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)

        # 2. Start verification tasks for devices that need it
        devices_to_verify = [
            device for device, result in zip(devices, results)
            if result.get('success') and device.device_type != 'shell'
        ]

        if self.config['enable_off_verification'] and devices_to_verify:
            asyncio.create_task(
                self.state_verifier.verify_devices_off(devices_to_verify)
            )

        return results

    async def _execute_fast(self, devices: list[Device], command: str) -> list[dict]:
        """Fast lane: Fire once, no verification"""
        tasks = [
            self._execute_single_device(device, command, 'fast')
            for device in devices
        ]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)

    async def _execute_single_device(self, device: Device, command: str, source: str) -> dict:
        """Execute command on single device"""
        manager = self.device_managers[device.device_type]

        start_time = time.time()
        success, new_state, error = await manager.set_power(device, command == 'on')
        duration = int((time.time() - start_time) * 1000)

        # Update database
        if success:
            await self.db.update_device_state(device.id, new_state)

        # Log command
        await self.db.log_command(
            device_id=device.id,
            command=command,
            source=source,
            success=success,
            error_message=error,
            duration_ms=duration
        )

        return {
            "device_id": device.id,
            "success": success,
            "state": new_state,
            "error": error,
            "duration_ms": duration
        }
```

**orchestrator/state_verifier.py:**
```python
class StateVerifier:
    """Handles OFF command verification with retries"""

    def __init__(self, db, device_managers, config):
        self.db = db
        self.device_managers = device_managers
        self.config = config
        self._active_verifications = {}  # device_id -> task

    async def verify_devices_off(self, devices: list[Device]):
        """Start verification task for multiple devices"""
        for device in devices:
            if device.id not in self._active_verifications:
                task = asyncio.create_task(self._verify_single_device(device))
                self._active_verifications[device.id] = task

    async def _verify_single_device(self, device: Device):
        """Verify a single device turned off"""
        device_config = self.config['device_types'][device.device_type]
        verify_config = device_config.get('off_verify')

        if not verify_config:
            return  # No verification for this device type

        interval = verify_config['interval_seconds']
        max_duration = verify_config['max_duration_seconds']
        retry_states = verify_config['retry_on_states']
        success_states = verify_config['success_states']

        manager = self.device_managers[device.device_type]

        start_time = time.time()
        attempts = 0

        try:
            while (time.time() - start_time) < max_duration:
                await asyncio.sleep(interval)
                attempts += 1

                # Check state
                success, state, error = await manager.get_state(device)

                if not success:
                    logger.warning(f"Verification check failed for {device.id}: {error}")
                    continue

                if state in success_states:
                    logger.info(f"Device {device.id} verified OFF after {attempts} checks")
                    await self.db.update_device_state(device.id, state)
                    return

                if state in retry_states:
                    # Still on or error - retry OFF command
                    logger.warning(f"Device {device.id} still in state {state}, resending OFF")
                    await manager.set_power(device, False)
                    await self.db.log_command(
                        device_id=device.id,
                        command='off',
                        source='verification',
                        success=True,
                        error_message=None,
                        duration_ms=0
                    )

            # Max duration exceeded
            logger.error(f"Device {device.id} failed to verify OFF after {max_duration}s")
            await self.db.update_device_state(device.id, -1)  # Mark as error

        finally:
            del self._active_verifications[device.id]
```

export function usePolling(interval: number = 5000) {
  const fetchState = async () => {
    const response = await api.state.getAllExhibitions();
    store.setState({ exhibitions: response.data });
  };

    targetType: 'exhibition' | 'artwork' | 'device',
    targetId: string,
    command: 'on' | 'off'

## Risk Mitigation

| Risk | Mitigation |
|------|------------|
| PJLink protocol blocking | Implement aggressive cooldowns (30s+), connection pooling |
| OFF verification failures | Log all retries, alert after max attempts, manual override |
| PostgreSQL migration issues | Backup SQLite, validate data integrity, rollback plan |
| Frontend polling overhead | Adjust interval based on load, implement backoff |
| ANEL network segmentation | Test runner connectivity, document network requirements |
| Config hot-reload race conditions | Lock config during reload, validate before applying |
| Device credential security | Encrypt config JSONB field, use environment variables |

✅ **ON commands stagger 1 second apart**

✅ **Fast lane bypasses verification**
✅ **Shell reboot commands excluded from bulk ON/OFF**
✅ **PJLink cooldown prevents blocking**
✅ **Hot-reloadable YAML config**
✅ **Modern React + TypeScript frontend**
✅ **PostgreSQL handles 1000+ devices**
✅ **Full admin interface for device management**

---

## Notes & Considerations

- **State values:** Keep existing -1/0/1/2/3 for compatibility
- **UUIDs:** Generate new UUIDs during migration, not reuse SQLite IDs
- **Credentials:** Consider encrypting device config JSONB in production
- **Monitoring:** Add Prometheus metrics for operation counts, durations, failures

- **API versioning:** Consider `/api/v1/...` for future compatibility
- **CORS:** Configure carefully for production deployment
- **Rate limiting:** Implement per-IP rate limits on public endpoints

---

This plan provides a complete roadmap from current Node.js microservices to a modern, maintainable Python monolith with clear separation of concerns, improved operational characteristics, and a much better developer experience.

### 3.3 Command Orchestrator
